questions.problem:
Given the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j,$ which of the following statements must be true?

- $∇\cdot F=0$
- $F$ is a source-free vector field
- Given two arbitrary curves ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2},$ we have ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

Note that $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.

- Statement III is false. Since $F$ is source-free, the result ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ is guaranteed only for curves with the same start and endpoints.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Given the vector field $F(x,y)=4xy\,i-2{y}^{2}\,j,$ which of the following statements must be true? 

- $∇\cdot F=0$
- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F$
- ${\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0$ along any closed curve $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

Note that $F(x,y)=4xy\,i-2{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=4xy$ and $Q(x,y)=-2{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4y.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=4y-4y=0.
$$

- Statements II and III are also true. Indeed, they are equivalent to statement I.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/67e73a2aec10d8052cc7c47bacb85046533929777401d399b124fe12bf82807c.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(2,1)$ and $B(2,4).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=-3\sqrt{y}\,i+3\sqrt{x}\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3\sqrt{y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\sqrt{x})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(2,1)$ to $B(2,4)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/ab4dc3ae0e3a62fc255a4bc066ae58c58f64546161466e4db474e39486492a53.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+t\cdot [(2\,i+4\,j)-(2\,i+\,j)] \\  & =2\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-3\sqrt{y}=-3\sqrt{3t+1}, \\ Q(x,y) & =3\sqrt{x}=3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3\sqrt{3t+1})\cdot (3)-(3\sqrt{2})\cdot (0)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-9(3t+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-2(3t+1)^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-14.
$$

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(5,1)$ to $B(2,4)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/d11be15ec3a455b3c19c52f64c767bbdd8bbd5eabf4c2243731eb5fc240b85d8.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5i+\,j+t\cdot [(2\,i+4j)-(5i+\,j)] \\  & =(-3t+5)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2y=-2(3t+1), \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=(-3t+5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t+5)=-3, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2(3t+1)\cdot (3)-{(-3t+5)}^{2}\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(27{t}^{2}-108t+69)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[9{t}^{3}-54{t}^{2}+69t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(9-54+69) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=24.
$$

r=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)=-2+2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/212435c94989d0553db86b8d39edae3a7905d41ef668bb33fa0a62bed99d5462.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

$$

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

$$
r(t)=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-2x=1-2(-1)=3, \\ Q(x,y) & =2y=2(2t-1)=4t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3)\cdot (2)-(4t-2)\cdot (0)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot {[t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/40bf4e64da0d4d9cb66e6e83d7275d4a44180a93341c413a5df720263469bfdc.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =4\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+2j)-(4\,j)] \\  & =5t\,i+(4-2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2xy=2(5t)(4-2t)=40t-20{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =-{y}^{2}=-(4-2t)^{2}=-16+16t-4{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)=5, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-2t)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((40t-20{t}^{2})\cdot (-2)-(-16+16t-4{t}^{2})\cdot (5))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,60{t}^{2}-160t+80\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[20{t}^{3}-80{t}^{2}+80t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=20.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/bfbb47ba32d4be8a72726c212cfca3fc61bf649bc4cf191b51ba1af4ab070c9b.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(2,0)$ and $B(-1,-2).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+2y)\,i+(x-y)\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free, and the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ can be parametrized as*

$$
r=(-3t+2)\,i+(-2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-y)=1-1=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/281eedbd33b31c7adc7b777379718d26832b9e5f6f8a18bc8a5a7fcd76a383bc.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(-3t+2)\,i+(-2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+2y=(-3t+2)+2(-2t)=-7t+2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x-y=(-3t+2)-(-2t)=-t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t+2)=-3, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-7t+2)\cdot (-2)-(-t+2)\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(14t-4)+(-3t+6)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(11t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{11}{2}{t}^{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{11}{2}+2) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=\frac{15}{2}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Source-Free Vector Fields
canonical_examples.problem:
Given the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{i} - 4x(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{j},$ which of the following statements must be true?

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F= 0$

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field

- For two arbitrary curves $C_1$ and $C_2,$ we have $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s \neq \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1,C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D=\mathbb{R}^2,$ where 

$$
P(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2),\qquad Q(x,y) = - 4x(x^2+y^2).
$$

Computing the partial derivatives, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=8xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-8xy.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
=
8xy + (-8xy) = 0.
$$

- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf F$ is source-free, we have that $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s$ for all curves *with the same start and endpoints*.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/f9b1b286210d694cd3786fe38190216da503bfa3223114f86c8706f810313e33.png)

The curve $C_1$ has endpoints $A(5,3)$ and $B(1,3).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\sqrt{y^3}\,\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\,\mathbf{j}
$$

 through $C_1$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector  $\mathbf{n}_1,$ as shown above. 

*Hint: You're given that $\mathbf F$ is source-free.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

First, notice that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,
$$

where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png)

Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5})-(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}.
$$
